name: Medicine and Human Body
description: Questions in the fields of: Anatomy and physiology, History of medicine, Diseases and immunology, Pharmacology and drugs, Genetics. Test your knowledge.

questions.question: Which London physician linked the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak to a water pump?
questions.explanation_correct: Snow compared cholera deaths and water sources in London and identified the Broad Street pump as a likely source.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Farr studied vital statistics; Snow is associated with the Broad Street pump investigation.

questions.question: What action did local officials take after John Snow presented evidence about the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak?
questions.explanation_correct: The pump handle was removed in September 1854 following Snow’s presentation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Penicillin was discovered decades later; it was not an intervention in the 1854 investigation.

questions.question: What did WHO establish in 1974 to broaden access to childhood vaccines?
questions.explanation_correct: WHO established the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1974 to broaden children’s access to vaccines.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Ottawa Charter addressed health promotion and was adopted later, in 1986.

questions.question: From which river did the two London water companies in Snow’s 1854 comparison draw their supplies?
questions.explanation_correct: Snow compared populations served by two companies drawing water from different intakes on the River Thames.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Seine flows through Paris; Snow compared London supplies drawn from the Thames.

questions.question: In which year did WHO declare smallpox eradicated worldwide?
questions.explanation_correct: WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 after an international programme of vaccination and surveillance.
questions.explanation_incorrect: In 1977 the last known naturally acquired case was reported; the global declaration followed in 1980.

questions.question: What is a spot map used for in an outbreak investigation?
options: Testing the sterility of surgical instruments
questions.explanation_correct: A spot map displays the geographic distribution of cases, helping investigators look for spatial patterns.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Genome sequencing characterizes genetic material, while a spot map shows where cases occurred.

questions.question: Which measure counts new cases arising in a population during a specified period?
questions.explanation_correct: Incidence concerns new cases during a defined interval; prevalence includes existing cases as well.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Prevalence includes existing cases; incidence concerns new cases during an interval.

questions.question: Which measure describes all existing cases of a condition in a population at a specified point or over a specified period?
questions.explanation_correct: Prevalence describes existing cases at a point in time, or cases present at any time during a defined period.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Incidence counts new cases, whereas prevalence also includes existing cases.

questions.question: What is an outbreak case definition?
options: A set of standard criteria for classifying cases
A method for sterilizing drinking water
questions.answer: A set of standard criteria for classifying cases
questions.explanation_correct: Investigators use standardized criteria, often including person, place and time, to classify cases consistently.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A case definition classifies cases using criteria; it does not prescribe treatment.

questions.question: What does public health surveillance involve?
options: A single laboratory test for one patient
Ongoing collection and analysis of health data
Automatic treatment of every exposed person
questions.answer: Ongoing collection and analysis of health data
questions.explanation_correct: Surveillance involves ongoing collection, analysis, interpretation and communication of health information.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A one-time test is not itself the ongoing population-level process of surveillance.

questions.question: In epidemiology, what does endemic mean?
options: Every case has been eliminated worldwide
A disease has spread across several continents
A condition is regularly present in a population or area
A laboratory test always gives a positive result
questions.answer: A condition is regularly present in a population or area
questions.explanation_correct: Endemic describes the usual ongoing presence of a disease or condition in a population or geographic area.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Global eradication is the permanent worldwide reduction of cases to zero, which is different from endemic presence.

questions.question: What is an epidemic?
options: Any single case of a genetic condition
A screening test performed every year
More cases than expected in a population, place and period
questions.answer: More cases than expected in a population, place and period
questions.explanation_correct: An epidemic or outbreak occurs when disease occurrence exceeds what is expected for a population, place and time.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An eradicated disease is no longer naturally present worldwide; an epidemic means occurrence exceeds expectations.

questions.question: Which disease is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae?
questions.explanation_correct: Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal infection caused by consuming food or water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites; Vibrio cholerae is a bacterium.

questions.question: Which public health infrastructure is especially important for preventing cholera transmission?
options: A larger supply of hearing aids
questions.explanation_correct: Safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene reduce exposure to waterborne infections including cholera.
questions.explanation_incorrect: X-ray equipment serves imaging; clean water and sanitation directly reduce exposure to contaminated water.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of oral rehydration solution for diarrhoeal illness?
questions.explanation_correct: Oral rehydration solution replaces fluid and salts lost through diarrhoea; severe dehydration may require intravenous fluids.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Antimicrobials may be needed in severe cases, but oral rehydration primarily replaces fluids and salts.

questions.question: Which physician developed the inactivated polio vaccine licensed in 1955?
questions.explanation_correct: Salk’s inactivated poliovirus vaccine was licensed in 1955; Sabin developed a live attenuated oral vaccine.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sabin developed an oral vaccine; Salk developed the inactivated vaccine.

questions.question: Which scientist developed a live attenuated oral polio vaccine?
questions.explanation_correct: Sabin’s oral polio vaccine uses weakened live poliovirus; Salk’s vaccine uses inactivated virus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Salk developed an inactivated injected vaccine; Sabin developed an oral live attenuated vaccine.

questions.question: Against which disease was the BCG vaccine introduced in 1921?
questions.explanation_correct: The Bacillus Calmette–Guérin vaccine was introduced in 1921 against tuberculosis.
questions.explanation_incorrect: BCG targets tuberculosis; it is not a cholera, measles or yellow fever vaccine.

questions.question: Which institution’s constitution entered into force on 7 April 1948?
questions.explanation_correct: The WHO Constitution entered into force on 7 April 1948, establishing the World Health Organization.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other organizations are separate institutions; WHO is the agency established by this constitution.

questions.question: What annual observance marks the date on which the WHO Constitution entered into force?
questions.explanation_correct: World Health Day is observed on 7 April, the date the WHO Constitution entered into force in 1948.
questions.explanation_incorrect: World No Tobacco Day and World AIDS Day are different health observances on other dates.

questions.question: What did WHO publish for the first time in 1977 to identify medicines needed by a basic health system?
options: The Model List of Essential Medicines
questions.answer: The Model List of Essential Medicines
questions.explanation_correct: The first WHO Model List of Essential Medicines was published in 1977.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Ottawa Charter was adopted in 1986; the essential medicines list began in 1977.

questions.question: Which 1978 conference produced the Declaration of Alma-Ata on primary health care?
options: The first International Conference on Health Promotion
The International Conference on Primary Health Care
questions.answer: The International Conference on Primary Health Care
questions.explanation_correct: The 1978 Alma-Ata conference placed primary health care at the centre of the Health for All goal.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The first International Conference on Health Promotion took place in Ottawa in 1986, rather than Alma-Ata in 1978.

questions.question: In which city was the 1986 Charter for Health Promotion adopted?
questions.explanation_correct: The first International Conference on Health Promotion adopted the Ottawa Charter in 1986.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alma-Ata hosted the 1978 primary health care conference; the 1986 health-promotion charter was adopted in Ottawa.

questions.question: What two approaches were central to WHO’s intensified smallpox eradication programme launched in 1967?
questions.explanation_correct: WHO’s intensified programme combined vaccination with surveillance to find and contain outbreaks.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections and do not eradicate smallpox, which is caused by a virus.

questions.question: In which country was the last known naturally acquired case of smallpox recorded in 1977?
questions.explanation_correct: WHO reports that the last known natural smallpox case occurred in Somalia in 1977; eradication was declared in 1980.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The eradication declaration occurred in 1980; the last known natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977.

questions.question: Which material did Edward Jenner use in his 1796 smallpox vaccination experiment?
questions.explanation_correct: Jenner used material from a cowpox sore when inoculating James Phipps in 1796.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rabies vaccination, insulin and penicillin belong to different parts of medical history.

questions.question: Which scientist is associated with the 1885 post-exposure vaccination of Joseph Meister against rabies?
questions.explanation_correct: WHO describes Pasteur’s 1885 course of rabies vaccination for Joseph Meister.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jenner worked on smallpox vaccination, while Salk developed an inactivated polio vaccine.

questions.question: What was variolation in the history of smallpox prevention?
options: Vaccination with an inactivated polio virus
Deliberate exposure to material from a smallpox case
questions.answer: Deliberate exposure to material from a smallpox case
questions.explanation_correct: Variolation exposed a person to material from a smallpox lesion; it carried a risk of disease.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Polio vaccination, water treatment and antibiotics are different interventions.

questions.question: What was the main purpose of the bifurcated needle used in the smallpox eradication campaign?
questions.explanation_correct: A bifurcated needle made smallpox vaccination simpler and economical in vaccine use.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other instruments and tests do not describe this vaccination tool.

questions.question: In the intensified smallpox campaign, what does ring vaccination mean?
options: Giving antibiotics to a whole city
Vaccinating contacts around an identified case
questions.answer: Vaccinating contacts around an identified case
questions.explanation_correct: Ring vaccination targets contacts and possible contacts around identified cases.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Airports, livestock and antibiotic treatment do not define this vaccination strategy.

questions.question: Which mineral was added to salt in the United States in 1924 to help prevent goitre?
questions.explanation_correct: Iodine was added to salt as a public-health measure against iodine-deficiency goitre.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Iron and calcium serve other nutritional roles; sodium is already a component of salt.

questions.question: Fortifying milk with which vitamin helped control rickets in the United States in the 1940s?
questions.explanation_correct: CDC identifies vitamin D fortification of milk as an important step in controlling rickets.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other vitamins have different nutritional functions.

questions.question: Pellagra is classically associated with inadequate intake of which nutrient?
questions.explanation_correct: Pellagra is a deficiency disease associated with insufficient niacin, also known as vitamin B3.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Iodine deficiency can cause goitre; the other vitamins are not niacin.

questions.question: Why was folic acid added to certain enriched cereal-grain products in the United States beginning in 1998?
options: To help prevent neural tube defects
To remove bacterial contamination from food
questions.answer: To help prevent neural tube defects
questions.explanation_correct: Folic-acid fortification was introduced to help prevent neural tube defects.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Iodised salt addresses iodine deficiency, and fortification does not sterilise food or treat malaria.

questions.question: What is food fortification?
options: Cooling food below its freezing point
Removing all water from a food
questions.explanation_correct: Fortification adds selected nutrients to foods, as in iodised salt.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Drying, pasteurisation and freezing are different food-processing approaches.

questions.question: In infectious-disease control, what does isolation generally mean?
options: Separating exposed people without known infection
Testing the acidity of drinking water
Separating people with suspected or confirmed infection
questions.answer: Separating people with suspected or confirmed infection
questions.explanation_correct: Isolation separates people with suspected or confirmed infection to limit transmission.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Quarantine generally concerns exposed people who may become infected.

questions.question: In infectious-disease control, what does quarantine generally mean?
options: Separating people who may have been exposed
Separating only confirmed cases for treatment
Measuring antibody levels in a laboratory
questions.answer: Separating people who may have been exposed
questions.explanation_correct: Quarantine separates people at increased risk after exposure; the exact rules vary by situation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Isolation generally refers to separating people with suspected or confirmed infection.

questions.question: Which activity seeks people who may have been exposed to someone with an infectious disease?
questions.explanation_correct: Contact tracing identifies people who may have been exposed to an infectious case.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Food fortification adds nutrients, while radiography and anaesthesia serve other purposes.

questions.question: Which environmental measure can reduce airborne infectious particles indoors by exchanging indoor air with outdoor air?
questions.explanation_correct: Ventilation supplies and removes air, which can dilute airborne particles when effective clean-air flow is provided.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vaccination and quarantine are different measures, while fortification concerns nutrients.

questions.question: Which action listed by WHO is a personal measure against infectious-disease transmission?
questions.explanation_correct: WHO lists hand hygiene among personal protective measures for infectious disease control.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Seawalls and irrigation address other problems; fortification adds nutrients to food.

questions.question: Which type of organism causes malaria?
options: A parasite of the genus Plasmodium
A bacterium of the genus Vibrio
questions.answer: A parasite of the genus Plasmodium
questions.explanation_correct: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by certain mosquitoes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vibrio cholerae causes cholera; dengue is a viral disease.

questions.question: Which mosquitoes transmit human malaria parasites?
questions.explanation_correct: Malaria parasites are transmitted through bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aedes mosquitoes transmit several viral infections; sandflies and ticks are different vectors.

questions.question: Which type of pathogen causes dengue?
questions.explanation_correct: Dengue is caused by dengue viruses and is transmitted to people by infected mosquitoes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bacteria, fungi and prions are different types of infectious agents.

questions.question: Which mosquito is a principal vector of dengue virus?
questions.explanation_correct: WHO identifies Aedes aegypti as a principal mosquito vector of dengue.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Anopheles mosquitoes are associated with malaria transmission; flies and lice are not Aedes mosquitoes.

questions.question: Which type of mosquito-control tool combines a physical bed barrier with an insecticide?
questions.explanation_correct: Insecticide-treated nets are one of WHO’s core malaria vector-control tools.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oral rehydration, X-rays and thermometers serve different functions.

questions.question: Which three researchers shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for penicillin?
questions.explanation_correct: The 1945 medicine prize recognised Alexander Fleming, Ernst Boris Chain and Howard Florey for penicillin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other groups are not the three 1945 medicine laureates.

questions.question: Which researcher received the 1901 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering X-rays?
questions.explanation_correct: Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of X-rays.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Koch, Curie and Pasteur made other contributions and were not the 1901 physics laureate.

questions.question: Which medicine was recognised by the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to Selman Waksman?
questions.explanation_correct: Waksman’s 1952 prize recognised the discovery of streptomycin, an antibiotic effective against tuberculosis.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Penicillin was recognised by the 1945 prize; insulin and aspirin are different medicines.

questions.question: Which disease was central to Ronald Ross’s research recognised by the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine?
questions.explanation_correct: The 1902 prize recognised Ross’s work showing how malaria enters the organism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dengue, smallpox and cholera are different infectious diseases.

questions.question: The Framingham Heart Study, launched in 1948, helped identify risk factors for which group of diseases?
questions.explanation_correct: CDC describes the Framingham Heart Study as a landmark in identifying cardiovascular risk factors.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The study addressed cardiovascular risk rather than only the narrow alternatives listed.

questions.question: Among people who have a disease, what does a test’s sensitivity measure?
options: The proportion of all tests that are positive
The proportion without disease who test negative
questions.explanation_correct: Sensitivity is the true-positive proportion among people who have the disease.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Specificity refers to negative results among people without the disease.

questions.question: Among people who do not have a disease, what does a test’s specificity measure?
options: The proportion of all participants who have the disease
The proportion with disease who test positive
questions.explanation_correct: Specificity is the true-negative proportion among people without the disease.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sensitivity instead measures positive results among people with the disease.

questions.question: In a disease test, what is a false positive result?
options: A negative result in a person with the disease
A positive result in a person with the disease
A negative result in a person without the disease
A positive result in a person without the disease
questions.answer: A positive result in a person without the disease
questions.explanation_correct: A false positive is a positive test result when the disease is absent.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A negative result despite disease is a false negative.

questions.question: In a disease test, what is a false negative result?
options: A negative result in a person without the disease
A positive result in a person with the disease
A negative result in a person with the disease
A positive result in a person without the disease
questions.answer: A negative result in a person with the disease
questions.explanation_correct: A false negative is a negative result despite the disease being present.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A positive result without disease is a false positive.

questions.question: What does the positive predictive value of a disease test describe?
options: The proportion of positive results from people who have the disease
The proportion of people with the disease who test negative
The proportion of all people who have the disease
The proportion of people without the disease who test negative
questions.answer: The proportion of positive results from people who have the disease
questions.explanation_correct: Positive predictive value is the proportion with disease among those who test positive.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Specificity concerns negative results among people without the disease.

questions.question: Which process is defined as destroying or eliminating all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores?
questions.explanation_correct: Sterilization is intended to eliminate all forms of microbial life, including spores.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cleaning removes soil; low-level disinfection cannot be relied upon to kill spores.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of cleaning a reusable instrument before disinfection or sterilization?
options: Making every instrument sterile by itself
Removing soil and organic material that can interfere with the process
questions.answer: Removing soil and organic material that can interfere with the process
questions.explanation_correct: Cleaning removes debris and organic material that can interfere with later disinfection or sterilization.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cleaning is an important first step but does not by itself guarantee sterility.

questions.question: What is an important difference between ordinary disinfection and sterilization?
options: Disinfection always removes all microbial life
Disinfection does not necessarily eliminate bacterial spores
Sterilization is simply the removal of visible dust
questions.answer: Disinfection does not necessarily eliminate bacterial spores
questions.explanation_correct: Disinfection reduces or eliminates many microorganisms but does not necessarily eliminate bacterial spores.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sterilization aims to eliminate all forms of microbial life.

questions.question: In infection-control terminology, where are disinfectants generally applied?
options: Living skin as a routine antiseptic
questions.explanation_correct: Disinfectants are generally used on inanimate objects and surfaces.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Antiseptics are germicides intended for application to living tissue or skin.

questions.question: In antibiotic resistance, what becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
questions.explanation_correct: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria change so an antibiotic is less effective against them.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Resistance refers to the microorganisms, not a person becoming resistant to medicine.

questions.question: Which type of infectious agent is not directly killed by antibacterial antibiotics?
questions.explanation_correct: Antibacterial antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Antiviral medicines and antibiotics target different kinds of infectious agents.

questions.question: Which practice contributes to the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance?
options: Using laboratory testing to guide treatment
questions.explanation_correct: Misuse and overuse of antimicrobials are important drivers of antimicrobial resistance.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Infection prevention and monitoring are tools used in the response to resistance.

questions.question: What does the One Health approach recognise in addressing antimicrobial resistance?
options: That only human hospitals influence resistance
That bacteria cannot move between species
The connections between human, animal and environmental health
That environmental contamination is unrelated to health
questions.answer: The connections between human, animal and environmental health
questions.explanation_correct: One Health recognises links among human, animal and environmental health.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Resistant microorganisms can move among people, animals and the environment.

questions.question: Which organ is primarily inflamed in viral hepatitis?
questions.explanation_correct: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver; several viruses can cause it.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kidney, thyroid and pancreas disorders are not what the term hepatitis denotes.

questions.question: Which is a common route of hepatitis A virus transmission?
options: The bite of an infected mosquito
Consumption of contaminated food or water
questions.answer: Consumption of contaminated food or water
questions.explanation_correct: Hepatitis A spreads by the faecal–oral route, including contaminated food or water and close person-to-person contact.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mosquito bites are important for other infections, such as dengue, not the usual route of hepatitis A.

questions.question: Which virus requires hepatitis B surface antigen to form its infectious envelope?
questions.explanation_correct: Hepatitis D virus uses hepatitis B surface antigen as its envelope; infection occurs with hepatitis B co-infection or in a person already infected with hepatitis B.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hepatitis A, influenza and measles viruses do not depend on hepatitis B surface antigen for their envelopes.

questions.question: How many main types of hepatitis viruses are conventionally named A through E?
questions.explanation_correct: The five main hepatitis viruses are named A, B, C, D and E.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The question refers to the five conventionally named main hepatitis virus types.

questions.question: Which form of immunity results when a person’s own immune system responds to vaccination?
questions.explanation_correct: Vaccination can stimulate the recipient’s immune system to produce active immunity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Passive immunity involves receiving preformed antibodies.

questions.question: Which form of immunity involves receiving preformed antibodies?
options: Active immunity produced by the recipient
questions.explanation_correct: Passive immunity can be acquired through the transfer of preformed antibodies.
questions.explanation_incorrect: In active immunity, protection is produced by the recipient’s own immune response.

questions.question: Which is an example of naturally acquired passive immunity in an infant?
options: The infant producing antibodies after vaccination
The infant’s skin acting as a physical barrier
questions.explanation_correct: Maternal antibodies can provide naturally acquired passive immunity to an infant.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A vaccine-induced immune response in the infant is an example of active immunity.

questions.question: Which description applies to an antigen recognised by an antibody?
options: A medicine that always kills bacteria
A substance specifically recognised by an antibody
questions.answer: A substance specifically recognised by an antibody
questions.explanation_correct: An antigen can be specifically recognised by an antibody; some antigens require a carrier to stimulate an immune response.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An antibiotic is a medicine and a surgical instrument is a tool; neither term defines an antigen.

questions.question: In a randomized controlled trial, how are participants assigned to study groups?
options: By allowing each participant to select the treatment
Only according to the researcher’s preference
By chance using a random assignment method
questions.answer: By chance using a random assignment method
questions.explanation_correct: Randomization assigns participants to groups using a chance-based method.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Allowing researchers or participants to choose groups is not random assignment.

questions.question: What does blinding generally mean in a clinical trial?
options: Ending the trial before measuring any outcomes
Keeping specified people unaware of participants’ assigned interventions
Preventing participants from reading the consent form
Assigning all participants to the same treatment
questions.answer: Keeping specified people unaware of participants’ assigned interventions
questions.explanation_correct: Blinding keeps specified participants or study personnel unaware of treatment assignments.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Randomization assigns groups; blinding concerns who knows the assignments.

questions.question: In a controlled clinical trial, what can an active control group receive?
options: An established treatment used for comparison
questions.answer: An established treatment used for comparison
questions.explanation_correct: An active control may receive an established treatment for comparison with an investigational intervention.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A control group does not have to receive a placebo.

questions.question: Who received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering human blood groups?
questions.explanation_correct: Karl Landsteiner received the 1930 prize for his discovery of human blood groups.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Koch, Fleming and Waksman were recognised for different work.

questions.question: Which scientist received the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for investigations and discoveries concerning tuberculosis?
questions.explanation_correct: Koch was recognised for his work on tuberculosis.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pasteur, Ehrlich and Lister made other contributions to medicine.

questions.question: Which two scientists shared the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin?
options: Camillo Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal
questions.explanation_correct: Banting and Macleod shared the 1923 prize for the discovery of insulin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other pairs were recognised for different work.

questions.question: Willem Einthoven received the 1924 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work associated with which recording?
questions.explanation_correct: Einthoven was recognised for his work on the electrocardiogram, which records electrical activity of the heart.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An electroencephalogram records brain activity, while a radiograph uses X-rays.

questions.question: Which Russian physiologist received the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the physiology of digestion?
questions.explanation_correct: Pavlov was recognised in 1904 for work on the physiology of digestion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mechnikov was recognised for work on immunity, whereas Einthoven was recognised for electrocardiography.

questions.question: Which scientist received the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901 for work on serum therapy, especially against diphtheria?
questions.explanation_correct: Von Behring was recognised for serum therapy and its application against diphtheria.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Landsteiner was recognised for discovering human blood groups; Koch was recognised for tuberculosis research.

questions.question: Which two scientists shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the structure of the nervous system?
options: Camillo Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal
questions.answer: Camillo Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal
questions.explanation_correct: Golgi and Ramón y Cajal shared the 1906 award for work on the structure of the nervous system.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Banting and Macleod were recognised for insulin; Fleming and Chain shared a later prize for penicillin.

questions.question: For research on the transmission of which disease by body lice did Charles Nicolle receive the 1928 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine?
questions.explanation_correct: Nicolle was recognised for research on the role of body lice in transmitting typhus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, while cholera is associated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.

questions.question: Which researcher received a share of the 1943 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering vitamin K?
questions.explanation_correct: Henrik Dam was recognised for discovering vitamin K; Edward Doisy shared the prize for work on its chemical nature.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eijkman was recognised for work associated with an antineuritic vitamin, and Banting for insulin.

questions.question: For work relating to which signalling molecule did Furchgott, Ignarro and Murad share the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine?
questions.explanation_correct: The 1998 prize recognised discoveries concerning nitric oxide as a signalling molecule in the cardiovascular system.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The prize citation identifies nitric oxide, not insulin or the other listed molecules.

questions.question: Marshall and Warren received the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastritis and which other condition?
questions.explanation_correct: Marshall and Warren were recognised for discovering Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. Peptic ulcers can also have other causes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tuberculosis, malaria and cholera are different diseases with different causes.

questions.question: What public health measure did CDC list as helping prevent tooth decay in its review of 20th-century US achievements?
options: Removing all minerals from drinking water
questions.explanation_correct: CDC listed community water fluoridation as an achievement associated with prevention of dental caries.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Iodisation is associated with salt fortification; adding antibiotics to drinking water is not the measure identified.

questions.question: In which year did community water fluoridation begin in the United States, according to CDC’s review of the 20th century?
questions.explanation_correct: CDC dates the beginning of community water fluoridation in the United States to 1945.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other years are not the date given in the CDC historical review.

questions.question: What was the principal subject of the first US Surgeon General’s report on smoking and health, published in 1964?
questions.explanation_correct: The 1964 report addressed the health consequences of smoking and became a landmark in tobacco control.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Smallpox eradication, blood groups and insulin are distinct public-health and medical topics.

questions.question: Which workplace disease named by CDC is associated with inhaling coal-mine dust?
questions.explanation_correct: CDC identified coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, also called black lung, among occupational health concerns.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pellagra, scurvy and goitre are associated with different nutritional or metabolic problems.

questions.question: Which type of road-safety device did CDC identify as protecting vehicle occupants?
questions.explanation_correct: CDC listed greater use of safety belts among measures that helped improve motor-vehicle safety.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A hearing aid, radiation badge and air filter serve different purposes.

questions.question: What is the main subject of the WHO Framework Convention adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2003?
questions.explanation_correct: The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control was adopted in 2003 and entered into force in 2005.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Its scope is tobacco control rather than blood-group nomenclature or chemical naming.

questions.question: In what year did the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control enter into force?
questions.explanation_correct: The convention entered into force on 27 February 2005, after its adoption in 2003.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1980, 1990 and 2020 are not the convention’s entry-into-force year.

questions.question: Which international instrument provides a framework for countries to manage public-health events that can cross borders?
questions.explanation_correct: The International Health Regulations (2005) set out rights and obligations related to public-health risks with potential international implications.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Ottawa Charter concerns health promotion; the zoological code concerns scientific naming.

questions.question: Which WHO body adopted the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control in 2003?
questions.explanation_correct: The World Health Assembly adopted the treaty on 21 May 2003.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The International Olympic Committee is a sports organisation; the other bodies did not adopt this WHO convention.

questions.question: In a cohort study, what does a risk ratio compare?
options: The test sensitivity with the test specificity
Risk in a population with its average age
Risk in an exposed group with risk in an unexposed group
Number of doctors with number of nurses
questions.answer: Risk in an exposed group with risk in an unexposed group
questions.explanation_correct: A risk ratio divides the risk in the exposed group by the risk in the unexposed group.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sensitivity and specificity describe test performance, not the two risks used in a risk ratio.

questions.question: Which measure of association is commonly used in a case–control study, according to CDC’s field epidemiology guidance?
questions.explanation_correct: CDC identifies the odds ratio as the common measure of association for case–control data.
questions.explanation_incorrect: BMI and Apgar scores are measures with other purposes, not the case–control association measure asked for.

questions.question: What do cross-sectional surveys typically estimate by measuring existing cases at a given time?
options: Only the number of new cases during follow-up
Only the proportion of randomised participants
questions.explanation_correct: Cross-sectional surveys commonly measure prevalence, the occurrence of existing cases at a defined time.
questions.explanation_incorrect: New cases during follow-up contribute to incidence rather than point prevalence.

questions.question: In an outbreak investigation, how is an epidemic curve typically constructed?
options: By charting the price of medicines
By sorting cases only by surname
By plotting the number of cases by time of onset
questions.answer: By plotting the number of cases by time of onset
questions.explanation_correct: An epidemic curve displays cases according to the time at which illness began.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A genome and medicine prices do not provide the time distribution of case onset.

questions.question: What does the numerator of an outbreak attack rate generally count?
options: All hospital beds in a city
New cases in the specified population over the outbreak period
questions.answer: New cases in the specified population over the outbreak period
questions.explanation_correct: An attack rate is a form of incidence proportion describing new cases among a population at risk over a defined period.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The numerator counts cases, not available beds or all laboratory tests.

questions.question: In descriptive epidemiology, which three dimensions are traditionally used to characterise health events?
questions.explanation_correct: Descriptive epidemiology examines the distribution of health events by time, place and person.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The alternative lists are not the traditional three dimensions.

questions.question: Which disease was targeted by the 17D vaccine developed by Max Theiler and colleagues in the 1930s?
questions.explanation_correct: Theiler and colleagues developed the 17D vaccine against yellow fever in the 1930s.
questions.explanation_incorrect: BCG is a tuberculosis vaccine, while the historical smallpox vaccine targeted smallpox.

questions.question: Which type of pathogen causes measles?
questions.explanation_correct: Measles is caused by the measles virus, a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bacteria, protozoa and fungi are distinct types of organisms; none is the cause of measles.

questions.question: Who shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning a novel therapy against malaria?
questions.explanation_correct: Tu Youyou was recognised for discoveries concerning a novel therapy against malaria, including artemisinin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Marshall was recognised for work on Helicobacter pylori and Einthoven for electrocardiography.

questions.question: What did Barbara McClintock discover, as recognised by the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine?
questions.explanation_correct: McClintock was recognised for discovering mobile genetic elements, sometimes called transposable elements.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Blood groups, X-rays and penicillin were the subjects of different Nobel-recognised work.

questions.question: Which diagnostic method was recognised in the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to Allan Cormack and Godfrey Hounsfield?
questions.explanation_correct: Cormack and Hounsfield were recognised for developing computer-assisted tomography.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Electrocardiography records heart electrical activity; blood typing identifies blood-group characteristics.
